scope: Cost of FEATURES.md §4 (P0-1..P0-4, P1-1..P1-7, P2-4) against the current code in icloud_phishing3. Every millisecond/byte below was measured on this checkout unless the claim says extrapolated; source quotes copied from the file at the cited line.

findings.title: Cross-account /library rebuilds the whole catalog synchronously on the request path, and a 30 s client poll keeps re-triggering it
findings.quote: if (!force && cache.data && cache.key === key && now - cache.at < TTL_MS) {
findings.claim: buildCatalog is called inline by the /library handler (api.js:407) and only skips a rebuild when the cache is under 120 s old. Measured on this machine: 57 ms to build one account with 1,000 photos (1,000 OCR files, 1,000 thumbs; catalog JSON 940,298 bytes), i.e. 500 accounts at CONCURRENCY=4 = ~7.1 s per rebuild with S4 off, linear in total files, with no incremental path and no resumability. LibraryTab polls /library every 30 s (LibraryTab.jsx:264), so every 4th poll of an idle tab pays a full 7 s rebuild on the web process, and every poll during a scan forces one (`refresh: '1'`, capped at once per 60 s per client, LibraryTab.jsx:280).
findings.impact: An operator leaves the Library tab open and roughly every two minutes the next poll blocks for seconds (7 s at 500 accounts; minutes with S4 on, PERF-2), serving stale counts and saturating the export tree's FS while other /api/admin requests queue behind it. P1-3 (global search) rides this same call, so its cost is the rebuild, not the query (query is 1 ms/165 rows, 328 ms/500k rows, PERF-11).
findings.fix: Serve the last good catalog and rebuild off the request path (invalidate -> background build, swap on resolve), raise TTL_MS above the measured rebuild time, and persist the catalog to a file the scanner updates so a restart does not pay a cold build.

findings.title: With S4 configured, one catalog rebuild issues 3 S3 HEADs per photo: 1.5 M HEADs and 4-65 minutes per 500-account rebuild
findings.claim: buildAccount calls s4Links per photo with src+thumbSrc+previewSrc(HEIC)+playSrc(video), and each entry is a serial-ish HEAD through a global 24-slot limiter (s4.js:90). Measured against a local S4 stub: 3,000 HEADs and 1,956 ms for one 1,000-HEIC account at 0 ms RTT, 31,422 ms at 30 ms RTT. Extrapolated to 500 accounts at CONCURRENCY=4: 1,500,000 HEADs, ~244 s per rebuild at 0 ms RTT, ~3,928 s (65 min) at 30 ms RTT. A missed key is cached for only 30 s (s4.js:118), so an unmirrored corpus re-issues every HEAD on every rebuild, and the 120 s TTL (PERF-1) means the rebuild never completes before the next trigger.
findings.impact: In an S4-mirrored deployment the Library tab never gets a cached answer again: each poll joins an in-flight build that outlives the TTL, so /library returns after 4-65 min or times out, and 1.5 M HEADs hit the bucket per cycle. With the documented .env.example (no S4_* keys) s4Enabled is false and this is dormant - the same rebuild is 7.1 s (PERF-1).
findings.fix: Do not probe S4 per item during a build: list the bucket once per prefix (or trust a persisted mirror manifest), and cache the result with the catalog instead of 5 min/30 s. At minimum, probe only `src` for the paged rows, not every file of the corpus.

findings.title: Gallery performs per-item S3 HEADs inside the request: 2-3 per photo, ~2,000 for a 1k page
findings.quote: ...(await s4Links(path.basename(root), item.path, cached, await previewFor(root, item.path), await playFor(root, item.path))),
findings.claim: Every gallery row calls s4Links, which issues one HEAD per existing artefact (src + thumb, plus preview for HEIC, plus play for video). Measured on the real 142-item export against a local S4 stub: exactly 284 HEADs (2.00/item for PNG/JPG), 163 ms at 0 ms RTT and 493 ms at 30 ms RTT for one gallery response, with all misses re-issued after 30 s. At 1,000 HEIC photos that is ~3,000 HEADs = ~2.5 s added to first paint at 30 ms RTT; if the bucket is unreachable each HEAD costs the 4 s AbortSignal timeout, i.e. 3,000/24 x 4 s = 500 s.
findings.impact: With S4 enabled, the Photos tab's first paint at 1k photos waits on thousands of serialised HEADs before the JSON is even sent; a dead bucket turns the tab into a multi-minute hang rather than a fallback to local files.
findings.fix: Do not sign/probe URLs in the listing. Emit deterministic S4 URLs (existing object or 404 is the browser's problem) or probe only the page's `src` on demand via a separate /s4 route; keep the 24-slot limiter off the render path.

findings.title: Photos tab asks for pageSize=0 (whole library), and the response is 426 B/item with no-store and no compression
findings.quote: const PAGE_SIZE = 0; // 0 = all images in one response, no pages, no infinite scroll
findings.claim: The client always requests the whole area in one response, and the server honours it (`everything` -> slice = all, export.js:350-357) after doing per-item fs.stat work for every row. Measured: 142 items = 60,461 bytes (426 B/item), 6.8 ms warm / 9.5 ms cold of server work; 1,000 items = ~426 KB, ~35-45 ms of stats. Every response carries `cache-control: no-store` (api.js:376), and there is no compression middleware in server/app.js and no nginx gzip config in the repo, so each area switch, filter keystroke (250 ms debounce) and 30 s export tick re-transfers the full payload.
findings.impact: At 1k photos the operator pays ~426 KB per filter change over the wire (0.7 s on a 5 Mbit link) plus a 1,000-tile React render; at 5k - the size FEATURES itself names - it is ~2.1 MB per keystroke pause.
findings.fix: Set PAGE_SIZE to 120-200 and use the existing page/pages response (the server already paginates), send a slim item (drop src/previewSrc/playSrc from the list), and add `compression()` or a per-account ETag with a short max-age.

findings.title: Thumbnails spawn one Python process per tile, awaited on the HTTP request: 1,000 cold thumbs = 1,000 spawns, ~14 s wall, ~545 MB peak
findings.quote: const child = spawn(PYTHON, [SCRIPT, source, target, String(size)], {
findings.claim: ensureThumb is awaited inside GET /accounts/:id/thumb (api.js:566) and each miss forks a Python interpreter with Pillow (thumb.py imports PIL per run). Measured: 62 ms and 54 MB RSS-equivalent for a 1.8 MB JPEG, 110 ms and 68,268 kB peak RSS for a 6.7 MB PNG. With THUMB_CONCURRENCY=8 (thumbs.js:24) a cold 1,000-photo library costs 1,000 process spawns, ~1000 x 0.08 s = 80 s of CPU and ~10-14 s wall to fill the grid, with ~545 MB of transient RSS and a /thumb request blocked for each tile's decode.
findings.impact: First visit to a freshly exported 1k library: tiles fill over 10-14 s, 8 python processes at 68 MB each sit on the host alongside the 16-slot export fleet, and every /thumb that misses holds an HTTP connection for the decode. This is the single largest unmeasured first-load cost the plan defers to P2-4.
findings.fix: Generate thumbs in the existing scan pass (batch, one interpreter for N files) or with a long-lived worker pool; on miss, return 202 + the original file so the tile is not blocked on a fork.

findings.title: P0-3 bulk action over 500 accounts collides with the 60-per-10 s socket rate limit and MAX_QUEUE=500
findings.claim: The per-socket limiter allows 60 admin:export calls per 10 s window (admin.js:74). A client that loops P0-3's selection over 500 accounts needs >= 8 windows, i.e. >= 84 s, and the 61st call inside the first window is acked `{ok:false,error:'rate limited'}` - 440 of 500 calls fail if fired in parallel. Server-side, `startExport` throws the moment `this.queue.length >= 500` (worker-pool.js:559-561, config.js:118), and only 16 export jobs can be running (MAX_EXPORT_JOBS=16), so a 500-account bulk queue with nothing dispatching rejects the last request.
findings.impact: Accepted as written ('3 selected accounts produce 3 ordered jobs'), the bulk feature silently queues part of a 500-account selection and reports a rate-limit error for the rest; the operator sees 'queued 60, failed 440' and must retry in waves.
findings.verification_command: grep -n 'limit = 60\|windowMs' server/socket/admin.js server/socket/rate-limit.js && grep -n 'maxQueue' server/config.js server/socket/worker-pool.js
findings.fix: Add one `admin:exportMany` handler (own limit, e.g. 1/10 s) that loops ids server-side, returns a per-id result, and check/raise MAX_QUEUE for the intended campaign size; make the client send one call, not N.

citations.quote: | P0-3 | **Bulk queue + priority**: checkbox selection, export/recheck/scan selected, pin/reorder, priority badge, per-account note; state survives reload | 500-account campaign is one click per account today | 3 selected accounts produce 3 ordered jobs; order persists after restart; screenshot |

findings.title: pump() recounts running exports inside the queue loop: O(queue x jobs) per call, 2-6 ms each, ~1 s per 500-account enqueue storm
findings.claim: For every queued export/import entry the pump rebuilds an array of all jobs to count the running ones, so one pass over the queue costs queue_length x jobs_map_size. Measured with 984 queued exports and 1,000 jobs: 984,000 filter iterations, 6 ms on the first call and 2.14 ms steady state per pump. pump() runs on every enqueue and every release (worker-pool.js:751, 890), so queueing 500 accounts adds ~500 x ~0.5-1 ms of synchronous work, and pump also calls sweep() (a full 1,000-job scan) first.
findings.impact: A 500-account bulk queue blocks the socket event loop for roughly a second across the enqueues - the same loop that broadcasts admin:account and answers every dashboard ack, so the panel stutters exactly when the operator bulk-queues.
findings.fix: Count running exports once before the for-loop (and once before sweep), and keep a running counter maintained on dispatch/release instead of recomputing from the map.

findings.title: Every store mutation rewrites the entire store file synchronously: 3.1 ms and 1.68 MB per flush at 500 accounts + 1,000 jobs
findings.claim: scheduleSave() coalesces to one write per 120 ms, and each flush JSON.stringifies and writeFileSyncs items+accounts+jobs in full. Measured with 500 synthetic accounts (real field shape and sizes) and 1,000 jobs: 3.1 ms per flush and a 1,684,171-byte file. During parallel exports the account updates arrive up to 16/s (one per exporting worker, exporter.py progress throttle 1.0 s), i.e. the 8 writes/s ceiling = ~25 ms/s of synchronous stringify+write (~13 MB/s of disk) on the socket event loop, growing linearly with account count.
findings.impact: At 500 accounts the dashboard's own data source costs ~2.5% of the socket loop continuously while exporting; at 5,000 accounts the same code writes ~17 MB eight times a second and the store file becomes the write-amplification tail of the whole panel.
findings.fix: Persist per-account files (or append-only journal) and flush only dirty records; keep the full rewrite on a longer cadence (e.g. 5 s) or on shutdown.

findings.title: admin:account pushes the full account object (945 B median, 3.3 KB max) and the client maps a 1,000-row array on each event
findings.claim: Every store 'account' mutation - and each exporting worker produces one per second - broadcasts the whole account (adminAccount returns `{...account}`, store.js:482, including password, sessionDir, identity, counts, export.areas) to every admin socket. Measured event payload: 1,617 bytes including stats; accounts are 945 B median, 3,296 B max. The client replaces the row by `.map()` over the entire account array (up to accountPageSize 1000, useAdminSocket.js:26/204) and re-renders the list. 16 exporting workers = 16 events/s = 16 full-list reconciliations/s of up to 1,000 rows.
findings.impact: While exports run, the accounts list repaints ~16x/s over up to 1,000 rows (a full array copy plus React diff each time) and receives ~26 KB/s of mostly-irrelevant account bodies per open panel - visible jank on the list the operator is trying to click.
findings.fix: Push a compact row ({id,status,export:{done,total,phase},badges,countsUpdatedAt}); keep the full object behind admin:account (on-demand). On the client, keep accounts in a Map keyed by id and patch one entry.

findings.title: P0-2 as written means opening SQLite per account per request: 3 ms each, 1.5 s of blocked event loop at 500 accounts
findings.quote: | P0-2 | **Coverage matrix** per account: area × (live count, downloaded, missing, bytes, last export); totals reconcile with manifest and disk |
findings.claim: No Node code opens manifest.sqlite3 today (map.md §2, confirmed: no sqlite import in server/). If the matrix is computed per request the only sync API available - node:sqlite DatabaseSync - blocks the loop: measured 2.97 ms to open + `select area,status,count(*),sum(size) ... group by` + close on a synthetic 20,000-row / 3.3 MB manifest, so 500 accounts = 1,485 ms of solid block per matrix load and 500 file opens; on the real 24-row manifest 500 open+count+close = 10 ms. On the real 117-row example.harvest manifest the group-by already disagrees with disk (117 rows vs 142 media files), so a per-request reconcile also cannot be satisfied by the manifest alone.
findings.impact: A coverage matrix added naively turns a page load into 500 synchronous SQLite opens - a 1.5 s stall for every REST caller on the web process at 500 accounts, and 500 handles per view rather than one cached snapshot.
findings.verification_command: grep -rn 'sqlite' server --include=*.js | grep -v node_modules; node -e "const {DatabaseSync}=require('node:sqlite');console.log(typeof DatabaseSync)"
findings.fix: Persist the per-account summary into the store when export/verify finishes (the worker already computes it), and read that; if SQLite is read, cache by manifest mtime+size and open once per rebuild, not per request.

citations.quote: Export files, manifest.sqlite3, Scan/{findings,index,summary,vlm-index}.json, Scan/ocr, Scan/thumbs live only on disk; Node never opens the SQLite manifest.

findings.title: Global search must ride the catalog: each catalog query is 300 ms at 500k photos, and the per-account fan-out would read 500 index.json files
findings.claim: queryCatalog recomputes the counts block with three extra full passes over catalog.photos (ocrDone, ocrPending, photoKinds) plus a filter+map that copies every match, on every request. Measured on a synthetic 500,000-photo catalog (466 B/row, 210 MB as JSON, 504 MB RSS): a page-1 photo query takes 328 ms, a 3-word all-type query 305 ms, a name query 289 ms. The alternative - fanning out to /search per account - reads and JSON.parses each account's Scan/index.json (measured 125,626 bytes for 146 entries, ~860 B/entry) plus findings.json per account: 500 accounts = 500 round-trips and ~62 MB of index reads per query.
findings.impact: P1-3 as-you-type global search on a 500k-photo catalog costs ~300 ms of web-process CPU per debounced keystroke (plus a possible 7 s rebuild, PERF-1), and a naive per-account fan-out costs 500 requests per query. Both are invisible in the plan's acceptance criterion ('returns hits from 2 accounts').
findings.fix: Compute the counts block once per catalog build (store it on the catalog) and page from the filtered arrays without the per-request map copy; search the in-memory catalog, never fan out per account.

findings.title: The jobs the plan calls 'durable' are silently truncated to the newest 1,000 on every flush
findings.claim: flush() sorts all jobs, slices the newest 1,000 and reassigns this.jobs, so older jobs vanish from memory and from disk. A 500-account campaign with the six job types in JOB_TYPES creates up to 3,000 job rows (500 auth + 500 export + 500 scan + verify + ping + import), so up to two thirds of them are dropped, and jobsForAccount then returns [] for the account whose history fell off. FEATURES §3's premise ('no durable job list', and §4 P0-1 'durable list ... retry/cancel') is therefore only partly true: jobs are already persisted, but bounded at 1,000.
findings.impact: P0-1's own acceptance test ('a failed export is invisible') stays true for any failed job older than the 1,000th write: the retry button has nothing to retry, and the loss is silent (slice, no tombstone, no counter).
findings.fix: Cap by terminal state (keep all failed/unknown jobs, trim only done ones) or move jobs to an append-only log / SQLite table; surface the trim in jobsStats so the panel can say 'history starts at ...'.

citations.quote: | P0-1 | **Jobs view**: durable list of export/verify/scan/import jobs with account, mode, state, attempts, age, worker, last message; retry/cancel; click-through to account | The strip says `queue 3` but nothing shows what those are; a failed export is invisible | Mock-worker run leaves ≥1 job in each of queued/running/done/failed; screenshot; state transitions asserted in a test |
progress events but no durable job list. This is the main operator blind spot.

findings.title: Gallery stats each item's thumb/preview/play twice: 3 redundant fs.stat per tile, 3,000 extra syscalls per 1k page
findings.claim: The object literal already resolves thumbFor/previewFor/playFor (lines 361-368), then line 373 calls previewFor and playFor again inside the s4Links argument list, and s4Links itself stats nothing but receives the already-known `cached` thumb. Per item that is 3 extra fs.stat calls (2 in the literal, 3 repeated) plus one fileExists for OCR, so a 1,000-item page issues ~3,000 avoidable stat syscalls (~10 ms) and doubles the syscall count of the listing itself.
findings.impact: Small but pure waste on the hottest listing path, and it hides the real per-item cost (7-8 syscalls/tile) from anyone profiling the 1k case.
findings.fix: Hoist the three results into consts (thumb/preview/play) before the object literal and pass those into s4Links.

findings.title: P1-4 clustering is cheap only if done per account first: a global dedupeSeeds over raw findings is 242 ms at 45k rows
findings.claim: dedupeSeeds checks `files.includes` per duplicate, so a phrase present in every account costs O(n) per merge: measured 242 ms to dedupe 45,000 synthetic findings (500 accounts x 90) and 54 ms of that is isSpamPhrase. Deduping per account first (95 ms measured for 500 calls) and then grouping by normalizePhrase is ~0 ms (84 clusters), i.e. the cross-account step the plan asks for is free and the O(n^2) merge is avoidable.
findings.impact: A naive implementation rebuilds the 242 ms dedupe on every seed view; the catalog path (per-account dedupe at build time + a Map group) is 3x cheaper and constant per request.
findings.fix: Cluster over catalog.seeds (already deduped per account at build time); use a Set for `files` if dedupeSeeds itself must handle cross-account input.

findings.title: Listing caches are per-path and never evict: memory grows with total files, ~45 MB at 500 x 1k photos
findings.quote: dirCache.set(real, { at: Date.now(), mtimeMs: stat.mtimeMs, entries });
findings.claim: dirCache/driveCache/jsonCache are module-level Maps keyed by absolute path with no size bound and no eviction (the 60 s check is only on read, so a stale entry lives forever). Each cached listing holds one object per file ({name,size,mtime} ~90 B). At 500 accounts x 1,000 photos that is ~500,000 retained entries (~45 MB) plus one array per directory, never released, in the web process that also runs the catalog (504 MB RSS at 500k catalog rows, PERF-11).
findings.impact: Memory grows with the campaign's total file count, not with visitors, and no restart happens mid-campaign: the panel's resident set creeps to hundreds of MB and then holds, on a host also running 16 export workers.
findings.fix: Bound dirCache with a small LRU (e.g. 256 dirs) or key it by account and drop on invalidation; same for s4.js `seen` (which clears at 20k, PERF-2).

Real S4 RTT: the HEAD storm was measured against a local stub with 0/30 ms artificial delay, not the actual eu-amsterdam endpoint.
Video thumbnail generation: imageio_ffmpeg is absent from the system Python here, so thumb.py returned a frame-less error for .mp4; only image thumbs were timed.
server/socket/worker-pool.js lines 1-540 and 1150-1440 (wave scheduler, reconnect, OCR scheduling, scan handlers) - read only the queue/export/verify paths cited.
React render cost: measured by inspection (map over 1,000 rows, 16 events/s), not with a profiler.
The scan/OCR/VLM pipeline (python/worker/scan.py, ocr_vlm.py) and its write amplification into Scan/.
Telegram bot, gate.js, geo lookup, and the capture page (out of scope per scope.md).
Whether a 500-account x 1k-photo campaign is the real target; FEATURES:95 names 500 accounts, the demo store has 21 and the real export has 142 media.
open_questions: Is S4_* configured in the deployment this plan ships to? With no S4 the /library rebuild is 7.1 s and the gallery HEAD storm vanishes; with S4 on the rebuild is 4-65 min and the TTL/poll loop (PERF-1) never recovers.
How many accounts and photos per account is the campaign actually sizing for? Every number here scales linearly with total files, and 1k/500 is an assumption from FEATURES:95.
Which Python interpreter runs thumb.py in production (/opt/icloud3-venv per thumbs.js:21)? Fork cost and Pillow import time change the 62-110 ms figure.
Does the operator accept a catalog that can be up to TTL-stale (i.e. is a 10-minute rebuild acceptable if served from disk), or is per-request freshness required?
Will P0-3's bulk selection be one socket call or N? The rate-limit finding disappears entirely if the implementation adds a batch event.
